turns.prompt: My basil plants keep dying on the windowsill. Can you explain what basil actually needs?
turns.response:
Basil needs **sun, warmth, and moist soil that drains well**. A windowsill can offer the sunlight but still be too cold—especially overnight. ([rhs.org.uk](https://www.rhs.org.uk/herbs/basil/grow-your-own?utm_source=openai))

The essentials:

- **Proper sunlight.** Aim for roughly six hours of direct sun, rather than just a bright-looking room. A sunny, south-facing window is a good starting point in the Northern Hemisphere. ([eauclaire.extension.wisc.edu](https://eauclaire.extension.wisc.edu/files/2011/03/MiniHerbWorkshop2015.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- **Warmth without cold drafts.** Keep it away from cold window glass and chilly air coming through gaps. Basil is less tolerant of a cool windowsill than many other herbs. ([chicagobotanic.org](https://www.chicagobotanic.org/plantinfo/tips/growing_herbs_your_windowsill?utm_source=openai))
- **Moisture, not a swamp.** Check the soil rather than watering on a fixed schedule: let the surface begin to dry, then water thoroughly and let the excess drain. The pot needs drainage holes; don’t leave it standing in water. Roots need air as well as water. ([rhs.org.uk](https://www.rhs.org.uk/herbs/basil/grow-your-own?utm_source=openai))
- **Regular tip harvesting.** Pinch out growing tips rather than repeatedly stripping individual leaves; this encourages branching. Remove flower buds to keep it producing leaves. ([rhs.org.uk](https://www.rhs.org.uk/herbs/basil/grow-your-own?utm_source=openai))
- **A little feeding.** For indoor plants, a liquid fertilizer at half the label strength every four to six weeks is enough. More isn’t automatically better. ([extension.umn.edu](https://extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/yard-and-garden-problems/growing-basil?utm_source=openai))

What happens first with yours—do they wilt, turn yellow, or develop dark leaves?

turns.prompt: How often should I water it, and how do I tell if I'm overdoing it?
turns.response:
**Check it daily, but don’t automatically water daily.** Push a finger about an inch (2–3 cm) into the soil: if it’s still damp, wait; if that top layer feels dry, water. That’s more reliable than a fixed schedule. ([rhs.org.uk](https://www.rhs.org.uk/shows-events/rhs-urban-show/houseplant-profiles/houseplants-for-sunlight?utm_source=openai))

When you water, wet the soil thoroughly, let the excess drain out, and empty the saucer or outer pot. Avoid little daily top-ups that keep the roots constantly wet. ([soiltest.vt.edu](https://www.soiltest.vt.edu/content/pubs_ext_vt_edu/en/SPES/spes-804.html?utm_source=openai))

**Signs you may be overdoing it:**
- Leaves turn yellow or brown.
- The plant wilts **even though the soil is wet**—don’t assume every droop means thirst. These signs suggest overwatering but aren’t a diagnosis on their own. ([soiltest.vt.edu](https://www.soiltest.vt.edu/content/pubs_ext_vt_edu/en/SPES/spes-804.html?utm_source=openai))

If it’s damp and drooping, hold off on more water and check that the pot drains freely. Roots need air as well as moisture. ([ask.extension.org](https://ask.extension.org/kb/faq.php?id=904518&utm_source=openai))

turns.prompt: Is it worth trying to grow it from seed, or are supermarket pots fine to keep going?
turns.response:
**Supermarket pots are fine to keep going—I’d try that before starting from seed.** The catch is that one pot often contains lots of seedlings crammed together, rather than one plant. Splitting them gives them room to grow. ([tollbit.gardenersworld.com](https://tollbit.gardenersworld.com/how-to/grow-plants/how-to-make-five-plants-from-one-supermarket-basil?utm_source=openai))

- **For the quicker route:** gently divide a supermarket pot into several smaller clumps and repot them in fresh potting mix, using pots with drainage holes. You don’t need to untangle every individual seedling. ([tollbit.gardenersworld.com](https://tollbit.gardenersworld.com/how-to/grow-plants/how-to-make-five-plants-from-one-supermarket-basil?utm_source=openai))
- **For growing from seed:** it’s worth trying if you enjoy the process or want different varieties. Sow indoors in warmth, then move seedlings into their own pots once they have several leaves. Spring is a good starting point. ([rhs.org.uk](https://www.rhs.org.uk/herbs/basil/grow-your-own?utm_source=openai))

Either way, the same light and warmth requirements apply—starting from seed won’t solve a cold or poorly lit windowsill. So my vote is **split a bought pot first; seeds as a separate experiment**, rather than a rescue strategy. ([rhs.org.uk](https://www.rhs.org.uk/herbs/basil/grow-your-own?utm_source=openai))

turns.prompt: Could you suggest something quick for dinner tonight?
turns.response:
I’d go for **tomato, chickpea and pasta soup**—one pot, about 30 minutes, not much to keep track of tonight. ([bbcgoodfood.com](https://www.bbcgoodfood.com/recipes/orzo-tomato-soup))

For **two generous bowls**, my simplified version:
- Soften a chopped onion in olive oil, then add a chopped garlic clove.
- Add a tin each of chopped tomatoes and drained chickpeas, **100g small pasta** and **600ml vegetable stock**.
- Simmer until the pasta is tender, stirring occasionally; add water if it gets too thick.
- Season, then finish with a spoonful of pesto if you have it. Bread alongside. Adapted from Good Food’s recipe. ([bbcgoodfood.com](https://www.bbcgoodfood.com/recipes/orzo-tomato-soup))

Have you heard how your dad’s check-up went?

turns.prompt: Not yet, he's calling later. I don't think I have chickpeas or stock though.
turns.response:
Then let’s make it **tomato pasta instead**—no chickpeas or stock needed.

If you’ve got pasta and tinned tomatoes:
- Cook the pasta in salted water.
- Meanwhile, soften garlic or onion in a little oil, if you have either. Add the tomatoes and simmer while the pasta cooks.
- Toss together with a splash of the pasta water to loosen the sauce. Taste for salt and pepper; add cheese or pesto if available.

One less thing to sort out while you wait for his call.
